original_title: Can we stop delisting original games to force remasters?
summary_en: Publishers are increasingly delisting classic games, forcing fans to buy newer, often pricier remasters. This trend sparks frustration and raises questions about preserving gaming history.
ai_analysis: The debate over delisting original games to push remasters highlights a fundamental tension between preserving legacy content and capitalizing on updated versions, impacting player access and publisher revenue.

en.title: Why Publishers Are Killing Original Games for Remasters
en.summary: Publishers are increasingly delisting classic games, forcing fans to buy newer, often pricier remasters. This trend sparks frustration and raises questions about preserving gaming history.
en.body:
It’s a practice that leaves a sour taste in the mouth of any dedicated gamer: seeing a beloved classic disappear from digital storefronts, only to be replaced by a shiny, often more expensive, remaster. This isn't a new phenomenon, but it seems to be solidifying into an unfortunate industry norm. The latest example causing a stir is the upcoming delisting of the Xbox 360 version of **Toy Story 3** on September 29th. The reason? A remaster is on the horizon, making the original, perfectly playable $9.99 edition seemingly redundant in the eyes of publishers.

There’s nothing inherently wrong with the original **Toy Story 3** game; it remains fully playable and enjoyable. Publishers, however, seem to believe that a remaster, which will inevitably carry a higher price tag, is the only way forward. The underlying motivation is clear: ensure players purchase the newer version and prevent them from having a less polished, but cheaper, alternative. This strategy also mitigates the risk of negative comparisons if the remaster doesn't live up to expectations. We’ve seen this play out disastrously before, most notably with **Warcraft 3: Reforged**. When Blizzard launched the remaster, they not only removed the original **Reign of Chaos** and **The Frozen Throne** from sale but also forcibly updated existing copies. This move stripped out beloved features and crippled custom game functionality, leading to widespread player backlash and even a surge in piracy as fans sought out older, more functional versions of the game. The fallout from that decision still resonates today.

## The Community's Frustration

This trend has galvanized a significant portion of the gaming community, leading to movements like "Stop Killing Games" and even prompting legislative discussions in places like California and Brazil. Fans argue that digital delisting, especially when it’s to push a remaster, erodes gaming history and limits player choice. While some might concede that delisting is acceptable if it’s for a truly revolutionary overhaul, the current practice often feels more like a cash grab than a genuine preservation effort. The upcoming remasters of the **God of War Trilogy** and **Gungrave G.O.R.E.**, both slated for 2026, will undoubtedly bring renewed attention to this issue, depending on how their respective originals are handled.

## What's Next

As more remasters are announced, the pressure on publishers to maintain access to original titles will likely grow. Players will be watching closely to see if companies prioritize player choice and historical preservation or continue down the path of forced upgrades. Information regarding the exact plans for the original **God of War Trilogy** and other upcoming remasters is still developing.

content_raw: The practice of removing an original game so its remake or remaster, usually the latter, can then be sold as the sole edition of the game has always really irked me. For years now, publishers have been participating in doing this, and it seems that it’s essentially become an unfortunate norm in the industry. The most recent example is that of Toy Story 3 . As IGN writes, the Xbox 360 version of the game will be pulled from stores come Sept. 29 , all because a remaster is on the way and so the $9.99 version simply does not cut it anymore. Is there something inherently wrong with the original? No. Is it in any crucial way unplayable or hard to go through? Not really. Reforged stands as one of the worst examples of this practice ever. Image via Blizzard So why is it going away? The remaster is likely going to be pricier and thus require you to dish out additional cash to play it. Purchasing the original would also mean that you’d have something to fall back to if the remaster turns out to be bad and would then draw comparisons between the two, causing unnecessary bad PR. This has happened many times before. Remember Warcraft 3: Reforged ? Back when it launched, Blizzard decided it would remove the original Reign of Chaos and Frozen Throne from all storefronts, also actively replacing them by forcing players to update their original games, moving players from the old, standalones to a “unified” client between Reforged and them. The result of that was a massive fallout with players, who decided to literally pirate Warcraft 3 so they could continue playing on the most popular versions like 1.27, as Blizzard’s forced updates removed entire features from the original games that were missing from the remaster. To this day, the forcibly updated Warcraft 3 games lack all the features they had before Reforged ‘s launch, making it one of the most egregious cases of remasters replacing their originals. I feel like pure greed drives these choices. I mean, you’re just taking away something that was entirely playable and functional and depriving the market of a whole game simply because this new “version” has 4K resolution and widescreen scaling. Remakes at least tend to try and recreate the game and make it better in any way they can, but remasters simply brush off the dust and charge you $30 for it. The case of Reforged happened way back in 2019, but the practice itself has been running for many, many years and shows no signs of stopping. With the likes of Sony moving into an all-digital future, we can only expect this trend to continue. Once the original is gone from the store, that’s it. It’s gone forever. With physical media, no amount of corporate delisting can stop the discs from spinning, with players able to copy them however they see fit to continue preserving those original experiences.
